operational-example.copy: Use Badge when a compact count or status marker must make pending work, exceptions, or freshness visible without becoming the main action.

scenario.title: Exception queue
rationale: The marker is secondary to a surrounding component.
Counts and statuses stay compact enough for tabs, chips, cards, and tables.
Tone communicates operational meaning without replacing visible labels.

items.rule: Owns pill or dot shape, minimum size, and alignment.
Shows a short count, word, or indicator with no wrapping.
Maps info, success, warning, danger, or neutral meaning to system energy.
Belongs to a parent control or object and does not own navigation alone.

accessibility.statePrecedence: disabled, hidden, focus, hover, overflow, default
items: Expose the count or status through the parent accessible name.
Do not rely on color alone for warning or danger badges.
Keep dot badges decorative unless the parent name announces the status.
Cap large numbers with an overflow label such as 99+.
Hide empty badges instead of rendering a meaningless zero.

variants.copy: Badge variants describe marker shape and content density. Tone carries semantic meaning while the parent component owns the action.

states.copy: Badge states communicate visibility, overflow, focus association, and disabled parent context without changing the parent component.

variant-state-behavior.copy: Variant sets the badge shape; state controls visibility and parent context. Overflow and hidden states prevent misleading counts.

full-width.copy: Badge never stretches to full width. The parent surface may stretch, but the marker keeps intrinsic size and alignment.

responsive-layout-patterns.copy: Responsive layouts keep badges close to their parent label and avoid crowding dense mobile headers.

viewport-organization.copy: Use fewer badges in narrow viewports and reserve danger or warning markers for operational signals that need immediate scan value.

items.title: Phone
items.rule: Show one count beside the most important label.

items.title: Tablet
items.rule: Pair count and status when labels still fit.

items.title: Desktop
items.rule: Use badges in tables, tabs, and cards without replacing text.

playground.copy: Use the playground to test short labels, tone, state, and overflow before placing Badge inside tabs, chips, cards, or table rows.

api-foundations.copy: Badge API exposes compact marker content, tone, variant, and accessibility label while Design System foundations own shape, color, and state.

props.name: state
props.notes: Local display state: default, hover, focus, overflow, hidden, or disabled.

props.name: hidden
props.notes: Hides the badge when the parent state requires it.

props.name: icon
props.notes: Approved icon name for the icon badge variant.

props.name: ariaLabel
props.notes: Accessible meaning when visible text is not enough.

groups.title: Use
items: Use for compact counts and status markers.
Keep the parent label responsible for context.

groups.title: Avoid
items: Do not use Badge as a standalone action.
Do not rely on color alone for risk.
Do not place multiple badges where one label should explain state.

groups.title: Review
items: Confirm the parent accessible name includes the badge meaning.

rejectIf: Dot status has no accessible equivalent.

miel.copy: MIEL treats Badge as a compact marker attached to another component: the agent can choose count, tone, and overflow, while the human confirms meaning and risk.
canDecide: Use Badge for counts, freshness, status, or pending work attached to a parent.
Select tone when the semantic meaning is explicit.
Use overflow when counts can exceed available space.
mustAsk: The badge changes legal, financial, safety, or permission meaning.
The parent accessible name is unknown.
The marker might be mistaken for an action.
rejectIf: Badge is requested as a standalone button.
Color is the only signal for warning or danger.
The count or status has no source of truth.
miel.handoff: I am using Badge as a compact marker attached to a parent component. I need confirmation on the source count, semantic tone, and accessible wording.
